title: AT 90 YEARS OLD, SHE BECAME A MOTHER—BUT THE FIRST THING SHE DID WHEN GOD PROMISED HER A CHILD WAS LAUGH.
paragraphs: AT 90 YEARS OLD, SHE BECAME A MOTHER—BUT THE FIRST THING SHE DID WHEN GOD PROMISED HER A CHILD WAS LAUGH.

She had spent decades living with an empty womb. Her body had grown old. Her expectations had died. Yet the God she struggled to believe was about to turn her laughter of disbelief into a testimony of His faithfulness.
Imagine reaching an age when you no longer pray for the things you once cried yourself to sleep asking God for.
Not because you stopped believing in God.
But because somewhere between the unanswered prayers, the disappointments, the passing years, and the exhaustion of hoping, you quietly accepted that some things might never happen.
You learned to smile when other people received what you desperately wanted. You congratulated them. You celebrated with them. Then you went home carrying a grief that nobody else could see.
Perhaps you know exactly what that feels like.
Sarah's story began with a devastatingly simple statement in Genesis 11:30:
“But Sarai was barren; she had no child.”
The original Hebrew reads:
וַתְּהִי שָׂרַי עֲקָרָה אֵין לָהּ וָלָד
Vattehi Sarai aqarah, ein lah valad.
Literally, Sarah was barren; she had no child.

The Hebrew word עֲקָרָה (aqarah) means barren or unable to bear children. Scripture does not soften the reality of her condition. It establishes the human impossibility that makes God's subsequent intervention so extraordinary.
In the ancient world, childlessness could carry tremendous social stigma. Yet behind that cultural reality was a real woman whose longing remained unfulfilled for decades.
Sarah was not merely a character waiting for a miracle.
She was a human being living through the painful distance between what God had promised and what her circumstances seemed to permit.
And that distance can be one of the most difficult places to live.

God had promised Abraham descendants. Years passed. Abraham and Sarah grew older. Eventually, in Genesis 16, Sarah gave her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham in an attempt to obtain a child through her.
What followed was not a beautiful solution.
It was conflict, jealousy, mistreatment, suffering, and a deeply wounded household.
Hagar was not simply an obstacle in Sarah's testimony. She was a woman who suffered and whom God also saw, heard, and cared for.
The Bible does not conceal the damage that human impatience can cause. Nor does it pretend that people chosen by God are incapable of making terrible decisions.
Perhaps that is why Sarah's story feels so painfully familiar.
How many times have we tried to manufacture what we thought God should have provided?

How many relationships have we forced? How many compromises have we justified? How many decisions have we made out of desperation, only to discover that our attempts to escape suffering created suffering for someone else?
Sometimes, we become so desperate for an answer that we stop asking whether our methods honor God.
And still, God's covenant purposes were not defeated by Sarah's failures.
That is not permission to sin.
It is a revelation of grace.
By Genesis 18, Abraham and Sarah were old. Sarah was approaching ninety, and Scripture explicitly states that she was beyond the normal age of childbearing.
Then came the visitors.
Abraham welcomed them, offered hospitality, and stood nearby as they ate. Sarah was inside the tent when a promise was spoken that contradicted everything her aging body told her.
“I will certainly return unto thee according to the time of life; and, lo, Sarah thy wife shall have a son.” — Genesis 18:10
Sarah heard it.
And she laughed.
Not publicly. Not as an open declaration of rebellion. She laughed within herself.
Genesis 18:12 records:
וַתִּצְחַק שָׂרָה בְּקִרְבָּהּ
Vattitschaq Sarah beqirbah.
Literally, “And Sarah laughed within herself.”
The Hebrew expression בְּקִרְבָּהּ (beqirbah) communicates something occurring within her, inwardly.
Her laughter was hidden from the people around her.
But it was not hidden from God.
She questioned how such a thing could happen when both she and her husband had grown old.
And before we condemn Sarah too quickly, perhaps we should examine ourselves.
Have you ever said “Amen” while privately believing nothing would change?
Have you ever sung about God's power while silently wondering whether He had forgotten you?
Have you ever encouraged someone else to trust Jesus while struggling to trust Him with your own circumstances?
Have you ever prayed with your lips while your heart was already preparing for another disappointment?
There is a kind of laughter that has very little to do with happiness.
It is the laughter of someone who has been disappointed so many times that hope itself begins to feel dangerous.
Then the Lord asked Abraham why Sarah had laughed.
And what followed was one of the most profound questions in the entire Old Testament.
הֲיִפָּלֵא מֵיְהוָה דָּבָר
Hayippale meYHWH davar?
“Is any thing too hard for the LORD?” — Genesis 18:14
The Hebrew verb comes from the root פָּלָא (pala), associated with things that are extraordinary, wonderful, or beyond ordinary human capability.
The question confronts the assumption that human limitations must also be divine limitations.
Sarah was looking at what nature could no longer accomplish.
God was declaring what His sovereign power could accomplish.
But notice something essential.
God was not promising Sarah everything she might ever desire. He was reaffirming a specific promise that He Himself had made.
There is an enormous difference between trusting God's promises and expecting God to fulfill every personal ambition we attach His name to.
Faith is not the power to manipulate God.
Faith is trusting the character of God, even when we cannot control the outcome.

Not every barren woman will become pregnant. Not every illness will disappear in this lifetime. Not every broken relationship will be restored. Not every prayer will receive the answer we desperately want.
And none of those realities automatically means that someone lacks faith.
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane with perfect submission to the Father's will.
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42
Christian faith is not confidence that everything will happen according to our plans.
It is confidence that Jesus Christ remains worthy of our trust even when our plans fall apart.
Sarah's story becomes even more uncomfortable when God confronts her laughter.
She denies it.
“I laughed not; for she was afraid.” — Genesis 18:15
And the Lord answers:
“Nay; but thou didst laugh.”
There is something deeply revealing about that exchange.
Sarah was not only struggling with disbelief. She was now trying to hide it.
Fear had turned her inward struggle into an outward denial.
How often do we do the same thing?

We hide our doubts behind religious language. We hide our bitterness behind smiles. We hide our secret sins behind church attendance. We hide our spiritual exhaustion because we are afraid of what other Christians might think if they discovered how much we were struggling.
But the God who heard Sarah's silent laughter already knows what is happening inside you.
He knows the prayers you have stopped praying.
He knows the questions you are afraid to ask.
He knows the sins you keep trying to conceal.
He knows the difference between the person everyone sees and the person you become when nobody is watching.
And He calls you out of hiding—not because deception is harmless, but because genuine restoration begins with truth.
You do not need to pretend before the One who already knows everything.
Bring your unbelief to Christ.
Bring your shame.
Bring your disappointment.
Bring your repentance.
The man in Mark 9:24 cried out:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
Sometimes that is the most honest prayer a struggling believer can offer.

Not as a formula to unlock a miracle. Not as a performance for other people. Let it be an honest expression of your need for Jesus, and an encouragement to someone else who thought they were struggling alone.
Then came Genesis 21.
The chapter opens with words that deserve to be read slowly.
“And the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken.” — Genesis 21:1
The original Hebrew reads:
וַיהוָה פָּקַד אֶת־שָׂרָה כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמָר
VaYHWH paqad et-Sarah ka'asher amar.
The Hebrew verb פָּקַד (paqad), in this context, conveys God's attending to Sarah and acting on her behalf.
And the words ka'asher amar mean “as He had said.”
That is the foundation of the miracle.
Not Sarah's flawless faith.
Not Abraham's perfect obedience.
Not their ability to manipulate circumstances.
God acted according to His own word.
Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the appointed time God had spoken of.
Abraham was one hundred years old when Isaac was born, and Sarah was about ninety, according to the ages established in Genesis 17:17 and 21:5.
The woman who had laughed at the promise now held the child of promise.
And the child's name?
Isaac.
יִצְחָק — Yitschaq.
His name means “he laughs” or “he will laugh,” coming from the same Hebrew root associated with Sarah's earlier laughter.
Even Abraham had laughed when God first announced that Sarah would bear a son in Genesis 17:17.
Now laughter had become permanently woven into the identity of their child.
Sarah declared:
“God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me.” — Genesis 21:6
צְחֹק עָשָׂה לִי אֱלֹהִים
Tsechoq asah li Elohim.
Literally, “God has made laughter for me.”
The laughter that once expressed disbelief had become laughter of astonishment and joy.
The same woman.
The same God.
But an entirely different reason to laugh.
What a remarkable reversal.
God did not need to erase Sarah's earlier failure from Scripture to demonstrate His faithfulness. Her doubt remained part of the recorded story, alongside the fulfillment of His promise.
Her weakness did not receive the final word.
God's faithfulness did.
And this is where Sarah's story becomes something far greater than an extraordinary account of motherhood.
Isaac was part of a covenant history that would ultimately lead to Jesus Christ.
In Galatians 3:16, Paul identifies Christ as the ultimate offspring to whom the Abrahamic promise points. Galatians 4:28 also describes believers as children of promise, like Isaac.
The story was never merely about an elderly couple receiving a child.
It belonged to the unfolding history of God's redemptive purposes.
Generations later, another human impossibility would confront another woman.
When Mary asked how she could conceive while still a virgin, the angel declared in Luke 1:37:
ὅτι οὐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πᾶν ῥῆμα
Hoti ouk adynatēsei para tou Theou pan rhēma.
The Greek communicates that no word from God will be impossible.
The language echoes the extraordinary question God asked concerning Sarah in Genesis 18:14.

Sarah's conception and Mary's conception were distinct miracles. Sarah conceived in her old age through her marriage to Abraham; Mary conceived Jesus by the power of the Holy Spirit while still a virgin.
Yet both testify to a God whose purposes are not defeated by human impossibility.
And through Jesus Christ came the greatest demonstration of divine grace.
Humanity was not merely disappointed.
Humanity was spiritually dead in sin.
We could not purchase our forgiveness. We could not erase our guilt through religious activity. We could not make ourselves righteous before a holy God through our own efforts.
So Jesus came.
He lived without sin.
He bore our sins upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The resurrection was not merely another inspirational reversal. It was Christ's victory over death and the foundation of the Christian hope.
The Gospel is not that God will give you everything you have ever wanted.
The Gospel is that through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, sinners can receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
That is a greater miracle than any earthly dream coming true.
Perhaps your greatest need today is not for God to change your circumstances.
Perhaps it is for Christ to transform the person you have become while living through those circumstances.
Perhaps you have become bitter.
Perhaps disappointment has hardened you.
Perhaps you have been punishing people who had nothing to do with your wounds.
Perhaps you have been trying to control everything because you are terrified of being disappointed again.
Perhaps the years of waiting have exposed an idol you never realized you were worshiping.
You wanted the blessing so desperately that you slowly stopped seeking the One who blesses.
Come back to Jesus.
Not merely because He can change your situation, but because He is Lord, because He is worthy, and because there is no greater treasure than knowing Him.
Hebrews 11:11 remembers Sarah in connection with faith and the faithfulness of the One who promised.
The woman who once laughed in disbelief is remembered in Scripture's great testimony of faith.
Her earlier doubt was real.
But it was not the entirety of her story.
And neither must your worst chapter define the entirety of yours.
The Gospel does not pretend your past never happened. It offers forgiveness, redemption, and a new life in Christ.
Not because every consequence disappears.
Not because every earthly dream comes true.
But because sin, shame, failure, and even death do not have the final word over those who belong to Jesus Christ.
Return to it on the days when disappointment begins speaking louder than Scripture.

You may never know who reads it in the middle of a sleepless night, who finds encouragement through it, or who begins opening their Bible again because you decided not to keep this message to yourself.
Sharing biblical truth is one meaningful way to participate in encouraging others toward Christ.

We want to continue bringing Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and Christ-centered spiritual nourishment into a world that desperately needs more than temporary inspiration.
Behind every article, every devotional, every discipleship resource, and every effort to reach another person is work that requires time, commitment, and resources.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be a beautiful expression of stewardship and a way to glorify God through generosity.

It is not a payment for salvation, a guarantee of divine blessings, or a replacement for your responsibilities to your family and local church. God's grace cannot be purchased, and your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before Him.
But if you have the means and believe in the work we are doing, your consistent support can help us continue and expand it.
And before you leave, remember the elderly woman inside that tent.
The woman who laughed.
The woman who doubted.
The woman who was afraid to admit what God already knew.
The woman whose story became a testimony to the faithfulness of the Lord.
You may never experience the particular miracle Sarah experienced.
But you can know the same faithful God through Jesus Christ.
You can confess what you have been hiding.
You can repent of what you have been excusing.
You can surrender what you have been desperately trying to control.
You can receive forgiveness for the sins that have haunted your conscience.
And you can discover that even when life does not unfold according to your expectations, Christ remains sufficient.
Sarah thought her laughter belonged to the end of a dream. God made it part of the testimony of His faithfulness. Never mistake the limits of your understanding for the limits of your God.
